klo: Articulate strategic intent in relation to the organisation’s purpose, long-term value and stakeholder relevance.
Define a coherent future position and the organisational meaning of success.
Evaluate the consistency between strategic ambition, organisational identity and the realities of the operating environment.
Establish a shared strategic direction that supports consistent enterprise interpretation and decision-making.

sections.label: Facilitator Guide
sections.sub: Use this tab to prepare before each section. It contains the unit intent, key facilitation questions, and tone and watch points for the full unit.

guidance: ◆ Unit Intent

Unit 2 builds the direction every later unit depends on: a Strategic Intent Statement and a Success in Practice narrative co-created by the leadership team. The 3W1H framework gives intent its structure; the four SiP dimensions make success observable.

The Strategy Maturity Assessment and the SiP contributions carry the unit. Protect time for executives to hear each other’s role perspectives before the contributions are integrated into one shared view.
◆ Key Facilitation Questions
“Could every member of your executive team state your organisation’s strategic intent in the same words? Where would the versions differ?”
“What would a customer, an employee and a shareholder observe if your strategy were succeeding?”
“Which SiP dimension does your leadership team discuss least? What drift does that silence create?”
“Which of the 26 maturity areas surprised you most, and what corrective action does it demand?”
◆ Tone & Watch Points
Watch for: intent statements that describe activity. Push for the destination: “What position will the organisation hold when this is achieved?”
Watch for: one SiP dimension dominating the conversation, most often Enterprise Value. Ask each role to speak for a dimension outside its function.
Application: the SiP Headline must be one sentence every leader can repeat. Test it by asking two participants to recite it back.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Interrogative Anchor · What is strategy? What is strategic intent? What is Success in Practice?
slo: Articulate strategic intent in terms of what the organisation pursues, why, how and when.
Distinguish the direction an organisation sets from the future position that defines its success.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1 · Awareness

Section intent: This section establishes the conceptual bedrock of the entire unit. Before any co-creation can happen, participants must share a single, precise definition of strategy and understand its three building blocks: the master definition, the 3W1H framework, and Success in Practice. Do not rush this. Every word in the master definition has strategic consequence.

Opening the session: Before showing any content, ask participants — "Write your definition of strategy in one sentence — right now, without consulting anyone." Collect 3–4 responses. Note the differences on a whiteboard. This gap between answers is exactly the problem this unit solves. Use it as the opening provocation.
Suggested section time: 25–35 minutes across all three sections.
Facilitator Script

Before this organisation can define where it is going, leaders must agree on what strategy actually means in the precise operational sense that makes every subsequent decision coherent. Open by asking: "If I asked each of you to write your definition of strategy on a card right now — would they match?" The gap between answers is the problem this unit solves.

parts.title: 1.1 — Strategy Master Definition
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1

Directing participants through the 7 concepts: Ask participants to expand each concept card individually and read it before moving to the next. Allow 3–4 minutes of individual reading. Then ask: "Which of these seven concepts is least visible in how your organisation currently talks about strategy?"

Key concept to linger on: The distinction between Thinking & Logic (OUTPUT concept) and Process (structured container). Most organisations have process but neglect thinking quality — the definition forces participants to see this gap.

The Value Triad (Creates · Delivers · Sustains): Draw explicit attention to this concept. Ask: "Is your current strategy as strong on Sustains as it is on Creates and Delivers? Where is the investment in sustainability of value?" This often surfaces an uncomfortable silence.
Suggested time: 8–10 minutes.
content: "Strategy is the output of iterative thinking, logic and process to determine what, why, how and when an organisation creates, delivers and sustains value to its stakeholders while navigating the forces within its operating environment."
Every word carries strategic weight. Expand each concept below.

parts.title: 1.2 — Strategic Intent: The 3W1H Framework
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2

Before opening the tabs: Draw attention to the Critical Insight box — "Most strategies fail because HOW and WHEN are underdeveloped." Ask participants to rate their organisation on each dimension privately (1–5) before exploring the content. This creates a diagnostic baseline.

Directing through the 4 dimension tabs: Walk through WHAT, WHY, HOW, WHEN one at a time as a group. For each, ask one diagnostic question from the content and take 2–3 responses. The HOW and WHEN tabs typically reveal the most significant gaps — give them additional time.

HOW tab — key facilitation moment: Ask: "Does your operating model currently match your strategy — or is it a legacy structure that predates your current direction?" This often opens the most honest conversation of the entire Awareness section.
WHEN tab: Ask: "Have you actually mapped the sequence of moves needed to achieve your strategy — or does the plan treat all initiatives as running in parallel?"
Suggested time: 10–12 minutes.
content: Critical Insight: Most strategies fail because HOW and WHEN are underdeveloped. HOW must include the full operating model and capability architecture. WHEN must address market timing, pivot triggers, and sequencing.
Dimension 1
WHAT
Dimension 2
WHY
Dimension 3
HOW
Dimension 4
WHEN
Without a clear strategic intent, every strategy discussion reverts to function-level interpretation. Strategic intent is the decision filter through which all other choices pass.

parts.title: 1.3 — Success in Practice (SiP): From Intent to Future Reality
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3

The critical facilitation shift: This section asks participants to make a mental move from planning to experiencing. Explicitly name this shift before entering the content — "We are no longer asking 'What are we going to do?' We are asking: if it has already worked, what does the organisation look like?" Insist on present tense throughout any discussion.

The four observable domains: Walk through WHAT→, WHY→, HOW→, WHEN→ and ask participants to briefly describe what their organisation looks like in each domain today. Note the gaps — this is a preview of the SiP exercise that follows in the Integration section.

Headline vs Storyline distinction: Ask: "Does your organisation currently have a Headline — one sentence everyone repeats? If not, what does that tell you about strategic alignment?" Then: "Could every person in this room write one consistent Storyline — or would you get ten different versions?"

Closing Awareness: After section 1.3, pause before moving to Intelligence. Ask participants — "What is one word that describes the gap between where your organisation currently is and the SiP you just imagined?" Capture the words — they will resurface in the Integration section.
Suggested time: 8–10 minutes.
The Critical Facilitation Move

"Before we move forward, we must be clear — this is the position we are committing to." Shift the question from "What are we going to do?" to "If this works, what will it look like in reality?" Position the team inside the future. Everything must be described in present tense as observable conditions.
content: The 3W1H must show up in lived form across four observable domains:
How the value is experienced by customers
Why stakeholders trust, choose, and advocate for you
How the organisation actually operates (rhythm, coordination, capability)
The pace, sequencing, and responsiveness visible in execution

The SiP narrative is anchored into four observable domains: Customer Experience & Value · Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm · People & Culture Dynamics · Enterprise Value Creation. This structure forces completeness, cross-functional alignment, and the elimination of functional bias.
"If our strategic intent is sound and our strategy works — what will the organisation actually look like, feel like, and perform like in practice?"
Headline — Strategic Vision Anchor
One sentence capturing the strategic destination. Leaders repeat it in meetings, town halls, and board discussions. Signals the destination without describing the route.
Storyline — Strategic Narrative
A narrative of how the organisation operates when success has been achieved, structured across four observable future-reality dimensions. Leaders describe an operating reality they intend to build.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Strategic Intent Must Precede Success Definition
sections.sub: Ignition Point · Why must intent be clear before success can be described? Why must both be co-created?
slo: Explain why strategic intent and the meaning of success must be co-created by the leadership team.
Recognise how a shared direction filters decisions throughout execution.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2 · Intelligence

Section intent: This section answers the "why bother?" question. Participants need to understand why co-creation is a strategic necessity — and why the Strategy Engine's three components must all be active for strategy to be durable. This section is the ignition point for the Integration section work that follows.

Transition from Section 1: Open with — "In Section 1 we established what strategy is. Now the question is: why does it so often fail to hold? The answer is almost never lack of intelligence or effort. It is almost always a failure of co-creation, thinking quality, or iteration discipline."
Suggested section time: 20–25 minutes.

parts.title: 2.1 — Why Intent and SiP Must Be Co-Created
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2.1

Opening the section: Before reading the content, ask participants — "Was your current strategic direction genuinely co-created by the leadership team — or was it shaped at the top and distributed downward?" Take 3–4 honest responses. Then read the three bullet points on screen and ask: "Which of these three results is most absent from your current strategy process?"

Key distinction to make explicit: "Compliance" versus "genuine shared construction." Ask: "Can you tell the difference in your organisation between a leader who is aligned and a leader who has complied? What does that difference look like in execution?"

Closing insight: Emphasise the last line — "This is the defining shift Unit 2 is designed to produce." Tell participants: everything in the Integration section section is designed to create the conditions for this shift in their own team, today.
Suggested time: 7–8 minutes.
content: The Strategic Intent Statement and SiP are co-created by the leadership team. This is a strategic requirement.
Leaders agree on the destination through genuine shared construction.
Trade-offs become visible early — the tensions between functions surface in the room, before execution.
Collective ownership is built — the only ownership that sustains during execution pressure.
When executives participate in shaping both outputs, strategy moves from individual interpretation to shared strategic imagination. This is the defining shift Unit 2 is designed to produce.

parts.title: 2.2 — The Strategy Engine: Thinking · Process · Iteration
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2.2

Directing through the three layer tabs: Walk through each layer — Thinking Logic, Process, Iterative Nature — one at a time. For each, read the "Where it fails" content aloud and ask: "Does this failure mode sound familiar in your organisation?"

The critical red box: Draw explicit attention to the red highlight — "Most focus heavily on Process, add some Iteration, and largely ignore Thinking Logic." Ask participants: "Where would you honestly place your organisation on this spectrum right now?" Allow 2–3 candid responses.

Thinking Logic vs Process: This distinction often surprises participants. The insight is that well-structured process can execute a wrong strategy efficiently. Ask: "Can you think of a time when your strategy process was rigorous but reached the wrong conclusion — and how long did it take to recognise that?"
Iterative Nature: Ask: "How often does your organisation genuinely revisit and revise its strategy based on new evidence — versus defending a settled position?"
Suggested time: 8–10 minutes.
content: Strategy is the output of three interlocked components that must run simultaneously. Confusion between these components is itself a strategic failure mode.
Layer 1
Thinking Logic
Layer 2
Process
Layer 3
Iterative Nature

Where Most Organisations Fail: Most focus heavily on Process (frameworks, templates), add some Iteration (strategy days, quarterly reviews), and largely ignore Thinking Logic — the quality of the reasoning itself. The result: well-structured, regularly reviewed, genuinely wrong decisions.

parts.title: 2.3 — Role of Intent & SiP in the S2R® Architecture
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2.3

Purpose of this section: This section connects Unit 2 to the rest of the S2R® journey. It is important participants understand that what they are building today — the Intent Statement and SiP — will serve as the spine of every subsequent unit. Make this explicit.

Directing through the 3 architecture functions: This content is rendered dynamically. Walk through each function — Strategic Alignment, Decision Filter, Execution Coherence — and for each, read the Strategic Intent and SiP columns. Ask: "Where does your organisation currently lack this function — and what are the consequences?"

Decision Filter — key facilitation point: Ask participants — "When a new initiative appears on your agenda, what filter do you currently run it through? Is there a shared filter — or does it depend on who is in the room?" This surfaces the practical cost of not having a clear Intent and SiP.

Closing Intelligence: Before moving to Section 3, summarise — "We now know what strategy is, and why co-creation and the full Engine are essential. Section 3 tells us where — in the actual life of an organisation — intent most commonly falls apart."
Suggested time: 5–7 minutes.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Intent Fragments & How SiP Reveals It
sections.sub: Locate Hot Zones · Where does strategic intent fragment? How do SiP dimensions make fragmentation visible?
slo: Identify the observable signals that show whether the intended future position is being realised.
Recognise where the dominance of a single perspective causes strategic intent to drift.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3 · Extrapolating

Section intent: This section moves from concept to diagnostic. Participants learn the four observable SiP dimensions in detail — and then see how imbalance in any one dimension produces predictable failure patterns (the Flammables). This section is the bridge between understanding the framework and applying it in the Integration section.

Framing for participants: Open with — "Strategic intent fragments predictably — at specific points and in specific ways. This section maps those points and gives you the diagnostic tools to find them in your own organisation."
Suggested section time: 20–25 minutes.

parts.title: 3.1 — The Four SiP Dimensions: Observable Indicators
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3.1

Directing through the dimension tabs: Walk through each dimension — D1 Customer Experience, D2 Operational Capability, D3 People & Culture, D4 Enterprise Value — one at a time. For each, expand 2–3 indicator rows and ask participants: "In your organisation — is this indicator in the 'What good looks like' column, or the 'What's missing' column?"

D1 — Customer Experience: Focus on the CARE model (Connection, Access, Results, Effort). Ask: "Which of these four value types does your organisation deliver most consistently — and which is the most exposed gap?"

D2 — Operational Capability: Ask: "Does your organisation have Priority Clarity — can every leader in this room state the top three priorities without checking a document, and would the answers match?" Allow the discomfort if answers diverge.
D3 — People & Culture: Ask: "What is the Dialogue Quality in your strategy meetings — honest challenge or performative consensus?"
D4 — Enterprise Value: Ask: "Is your growth strategy-driven or market-driven? Can you trace your current growth to specific strategic choices?"
Suggested time: 12–14 minutes.
content: Each SiP dimension is a multidimensional observable reality. These are the specific signals that tell an executive team whether the strategy is working in that domain.
D1 · Customer Experience & Value
D2 · Operational Capability
D3 · People & Culture
D4 · Enterprise Value

parts.title: 3.2 — SiP Flammables: Where Imbalance Creates Drift
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3.2

Framing the Flammables: Explain — "When one executive function dominates the SiP narrative, the strategy becomes a functional ambition that no longer describes the enterprise. These four patterns show what that looks like — and they are all recognisable."

Directing through the four flammables: Read each pattern aloud. After each one, ask: "Raise your hand if you have seen this in an organisation you have worked in." Expect near-universal recognition. Then ask: "Which of these four is your organisation most at risk of right now?"

Connecting to the Integration section: After all four have been explored, tell participants — "In the Integration section, each of you will contribute a SiP from your assigned executive role. The Flammables are your quality check — use them to audit whether your own contribution is balanced or skewed."

The existing facilitator guidance below applies here: After each leader describes their SiP perspective in the Integration section, ask the room which Flammable their perspective risks creating. Naming the imbalance explicitly is what prevents it from taking hold.
Suggested time: 6–8 minutes.
Facilitator Move
After each leader describes their SiP perspective, ask the room: "Which of these four flammables does this perspective risk creating?" Name the imbalance explicitly.
content: When one dimension dominates the SiP narrative, the strategy narrows into a functional ambition that no longer describes the enterprise.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.sub: Collective Intelligence of Execution · Leadership biases · Strategy Maturity · SiP Exercise · Integration Synthesis
slo: Evaluate the organisation’s strategic maturity against the ambition it has set.
Contribute an enterprise perspective to a collective definition of success.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4 · Integration

Section intent: This is the production section. Everything in Awareness, Intelligence, and Extrapolating has been preparation for this. Four activities run in sequence: understanding executive role biases, completing the Strategy Maturity Assessment, contributing individual SiP narratives, and synthesising toward collective outputs. Allow sufficient time — this is the core deliverable of Unit 2.

Framing for participants: Open with — "We have spent the first three sections building the conceptual architecture. This section is where the organisation's actual strategic picture gets built — collectively, in this room, today. What you produce here will be the foundation for every subsequent unit."
Sequencing the four activities:
4.1 — Executive Role Perspectives (10–12 min): Understanding biases before the SiP exercise
4.2 — Strategy Maturity Assessment (15–20 min): Individual scoring, group debrief
4.3 — Collective SiP Exercise (20–30 min): Individual contribution, synthesis
Summary — Unit Summary debrief (8–10 min): What this unit produced
Suggested total section time: 55–75 minutes.

parts.title: 4.1 — Executive Leader Perspectives: Natural Biases & Integration Challenges
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4.1
Purpose before the SiP exercise: This section is a bias-awareness primer before the SiP exercise. Participants must understand their natural perspective before they can transcend it.

Directing participants: Ask each participant to click their assigned executive role card. Give them 2 minutes to read their role's bias and integration challenge. Then ask: "Does this description of your role's natural bias feel accurate? Where does it resonate most strongly?"

Group debrief: Ask 3–4 participants to read their "Integration Challenge" aloud. Then ask the full group — "If these biases all operate simultaneously in a SiP exercise — what happens to the collective picture? Which dimensions get over-represented and which get left behind?"
Key facilitation point: Emphasise that the goal is to make the functional bias visible so the collective can compensate for it. The integration challenge is structural information the group needs.
Suggested time: 10–12 minutes.
content: When executive leaders describe strategic intent, they naturally emphasise their domain. This produces multiple partial pictures that are each accurate — and collectively incomplete. The Integration section transforms these into one picture.

parts.title: 4.2 — Strategy Maturity Assessment: 26 Areas
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4.2

Setting up the assessment: Before participants begin scoring, read the instruction aloud — "Score the organisation as it actually is right now. Honest assessment is the only kind that is useful." Emphasise that this is a diagnostic tool.

Individual vs collective scoring: For maximum insight, ask each participant to score independently first — without discussion. Allow 8–10 minutes of silent individual scoring across all six groups. Then compare scores across the group. Significant divergence on the same item is itself a strategic finding — it signals that different leaders have fundamentally different views of organisational reality.
Group debrief after scoring: Use these three questions in sequence:
"Which group (A–F) scored lowest across the team — and was there consensus on that?"
"Where was the widest divergence in scores? What does that disagreement tell us?"
"What is the single most important corrective action this score points to in the next 90 days?"

Using the export function: Direct participants (or the lead facilitator) to use "Screen View" or "Save as PDF" to generate the maturity report. This becomes a baseline document for the organisation's S2R® journey — it should be retained and revisited at the end of the programme.

Score interpretation: 0–26 = Foundational Gaps (strategy is fragile, personality-dependent). 27–52 = Developing Capability (key dimensions present but integration incomplete). 53–78 = Strategic Maturity (strategy is embedded as organisational capability). Most first-time groups score in the 20–45 range — normalise this and focus on the direction of travel.
Suggested time: 15–20 minutes including individual scoring and group debrief.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete this activity in their own file. The content below is for your preparation.
content: The executive team assesses the organisation across 26 strategy components. Score: 0 = Not addressed · 1 = Partially · 2 = Substantially · 3 = Fully embedded.
Foundational Gaps
Strategy remains fragile and personality-dependent.
Developing Capability
Key dimensions present; integration incomplete.
Strategic Maturity

parts.title: 4.3 — Collective SiP Exercise: Four Dimensions per Executive Role
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4.3
This is the core deliverable of Unit 2. Everything prior has been preparation for this exercise. Protect the time — do not compress it.
Setting up the exercise:
Assign executive roles before participants begin — do not allow self-selection. The learning comes partly from being required to inhabit a perspective that is not naturally yours.
Remind participants: "Write in the present tense of the future: 'we have...', 'customers experience...'"
Reinforce the Flammable risk: "As you write, notice when you are defaulting to your functional comfort zone. Push yourself into the dimensions that feel less natural."

Individual writing time: Allow 10–12 minutes for each participant to complete all four dimensions from their assigned role. This must be done in silence — the independent perspective is what makes the synthesis valuable. Group discussion before individual writing contaminates the outputs.
Running the synthesis: After individual contributions are complete, use the "View All Responses" function to display contributions side by side. Facilitate the synthesis using four questions:
"Where do all perspectives converge? This is your strongest strategic signal."
"Where do perspectives compete or contradict? This is where trade-off decisions are needed."
"Which SiP dimension is least well-described across all contributions? This is your white space — who owns it?"
"Which functional perspective dominates the collective narrative? How do we rebalance?"

Producing the collective output: The facilitator (or a nominated scribe) drafts a single integrated SiP from the synthesis discussion. This draft becomes the working SiP for the organisation — it will be tested, refined, and embedded across subsequent units. It needs to be genuinely shared today; refinement follows in later units.
Suggested time: 20–30 minutes including individual writing, synthesis discussion, and collective draft.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete this activity in their own file. The content below is for your preparation.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE

After all leaders complete, lead a structured synthesis: identify convergence (where all align), tension (where perspectives compete), missing dimensions (where no leader adequately described the future state), and dominant bias (which functional perspective over-represents the narrative).
◆ PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants write the four SiP dimensions from their assigned role in Section 4.3 of their own file, in silence. When all have finished, lead the synthesis from their responses.
content: Each leader describes all four SiP dimensions from their assigned role's perspective, written in the present tense of the future — as if the strategy has already succeeded.

sections.label: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
sections.sub: The executive team uses the Strategy Maturity Assessment results to define corrective actions across the four SiP dimensions, then completes the CXO contribution table written in the present tense of the future.
slo: Define the actions needed to close the gap between current maturity and the intended future position.
Establish a shared statement of success that supports consistent enterprise decision-making.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5 · Application

Section intent: This is the synthesis and application section. Participants move from understanding and assessing (Sections 1–4) to producing two integrated outputs: corrective action priorities and a fully completed CXO × SiP table. The headline and storyline produced here become the destination anchor for the entire S2R® journey.
Sequencing the four activities:
5.1 — Corrective Actions (10–15 min): Each participant reviews their assessment score and identifies actions per SiP dimension
5.2 — CXO SiP Application Table (20–30 min): Each CXO completes their row in present-tense future language
5.3 — SiP Headline & Storyline (10–15 min): Individual contribution, then group synthesis
5.4 — Integration Summary (15–20 min): Facilitator leads synthesis of convergence, tension, missing dimensions, dominant bias
Suggested total section time: 55–80 minutes.

parts.title: 5.1 — Using Assessment Results: Defining Corrective Actions
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5.1

Opening the section: Ask participants to open Section 4.2 in a side window or navigate back to review their assessment score before completing this section. Say: "Your assessment revealed where your organisation's strategic capability is strongest and most fragile. This section asks you to convert those diagnostic results into specific corrective actions — the precise changes that must happen for your SiP to become real."

Key facilitation point: The corrective actions must be specific and cross-functional. Push back on vague responses like "improve communication" — ask: "Improve it how, between whom, and in what rhythm?"

Group debrief: After participants have completed their corrective actions, ask 3–4 to share the most critical action in each dimension. Note where multiple participants identify the same gap — this is a convergence point that strengthens the collective SiP.
Suggested time: 10–15 minutes.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete this activity in their own file. The content below is for your preparation.
content: Participants use their Strategy Maturity Assessment results from Section 4 to identify the most critical corrective actions required across the four SiP dimensions. The assessment score across all 26 areas reveals where the organisation's strategic capability is strongest — and where it is most fragile.

The corrective actions identified here become the inputs into the SiP Application Table in 5.2. Before completing their SiP dimensions, each participant should review their assessment results and identify the specific gaps that must be addressed for the strategy to succeed.
Assessment Score Reference
Group Assessment Score
Score reflects the group assessment from Section 4
Corrective Actions — Group Capture
Use this space to capture the group's collective corrective actions across the four dimensions as they emerge from the debrief.
D1 · Customer Experience & Value
What must change to close the gap between the current customer experience and the SiP vision?
D2 · Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm
What operational gaps must be closed for the strategy to execute reliably?
D3 · People & Culture Dynamics
What cultural and behavioural shifts are required to bring the SiP to life?
D4 · Enterprise Value Creation
What must be strengthened to ensure the strategy creates durable enterprise value?

parts.title: 5.2 — CXO SiP Application Table: All Executive Roles
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5.2

Purpose: This table captures each CXO's description of the four SiP dimensions from their assigned role's perspective. It is the primary deliverable of the Application section and produces the raw material for the integration synthesis in 5.4.

Directing the exercise: Ask each participant to select their assigned role and complete all four dimensions simultaneously. Enforce present-tense future language throughout — interrupt any responses that slip into planning or future-tense description.

Quality check: After each CXO completes their row, ask them to self-audit against the Flammable patterns from Section 3.2. Ask: "Which Flammable does your response risk creating? What would you add to balance it?"
Facilitator can record directly: Use the full table view below to capture group responses as they are shared verbally, or ask participants to enter their own responses from their screens.
Suggested time: 20–30 minutes.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete this activity in their own file. The content below is for your preparation.
◆ PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete their row of the CXO SiP Application Table in Section 5.2 of their own file.
content: Each executive leader describes the four SiP dimensions from the perspective of their assigned role. All responses must be written in the present tense of the future — as if the strategy has already succeeded.
Facilitator: After all CXO rows are completed, use the Integration Summary in Section 5.4 to identify convergence, tension, missing dimensions, and dominant bias across all contributions.

parts.title: 5.3 — SiP Headline & Storyline: Collective Synthesis
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5.3

The synthesis move: After all CXO rows in 5.2 are completed, invite each participant to distil their perspective into a Headline and a Storyline. Then — and this is the critical facilitation move — bring the group together to synthesise these individual contributions into one shared Headline and one co-owned Storyline.

Headline synthesis: Read all individual Headlines aloud. Ask the group: "What words appear in most headlines? What is the common destination we are all pointing at?" Draft a composite headline together — do not let one executive write it alone.
Storyline synthesis: Ask each CXO to read their Storyline aloud. Capture themes on a whiteboard across the four dimensions. The shared Storyline emerges from points of convergence.
Suggested time: 15–20 minutes.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete this activity in their own file. The content below is for your preparation.
content: Individual contributions from each CXO are synthesised here into one shared Strategic Intent Statement and one co-owned SiP Headline and Storyline.
Emerging Shared SiP Headline
One sentence. The strategic destination that the collective executive team agrees on. Synthesised from individual contributions.
Emerging Shared SiP Storyline
The collective narrative description of the future organisation, written in the present tense of the future across all four dimensions.

parts.title: 5.4 — Integration Summary: The Emerging Collective View
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5.4

The integration synthesis: This is the most important facilitation moment in the entire unit. After all CXO contributions are captured in 5.2 and 5.3, lead the group through a structured analysis of the four dimensions below. Do not rush this — the most valuable strategic insight often emerges in the tension and missing dimensions.

Sequencing the synthesis: Start with Convergence (build collective confidence), then move to Tension (surface productive disagreement), then Missing Dimensions (name the blind spots), then Dominant Bias (invite honest self-assessment from the dominant function). The order matters — starting with tension creates defensiveness that prevents the insight from landing.

Closing the unit: End with the question: "We have now described the organisation we intend to build. The gap between what we described and what we currently have — is that gap strategic or operational? And who in this room is accountable for closing it?"
Suggested time: 15–20 minutes.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Participants complete this activity in their own file. The content below is for your preparation.
content: The facilitator leads a structured synthesis to identify the four dimensions of the emerging collective view across all CXO contributions.
Points of Convergence
Where all CXO descriptions aligned. What the organisation consistently looks like across all perspectives.
Points of Tension
Where perspectives contradicted or competed. Which functions described incompatible futures.
Missing Dimensions
Which SiP dimensions were inadequately described by any CXO. The collective blind spot.
Dominant Bias
Which functional perspective was over-represented. What this reveals about collective strategic blind spots.
📋Facilitator Closing Note
Record the single most important strategic insight that emerged from the Application — the insight the group did not have at the start of the session.

parts.title: Unit Summary
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Unit Summary

Closing the unit: Expand the summary accordion and read each of the four sections aloud, or ask participants to read them in turn. The summary is deliberately concise — its role is to crystallise the arc of the unit.

Return to the opening question: Go back to the definitions participants wrote at the start of Awareness. Ask 2–3 participants — "Read your original definition of strategy. What would you change in it now — and why?" The difference between their opening answer and their closing answer is the measure of what Unit 2 produced.
Tangible outputs check: Before closing, confirm with the group that the following have been produced or are in progress:
A collective Strategy Maturity Assessment score (with the lowest group identified)
Individual SiP contributions from all assigned executive roles
A working draft of the collective SiP (Headline + Storyline)

Closing commitment: Ask each participant to complete this sentence privately — "Based on what Unit 2 revealed, the one thing I am committed to doing differently before our next session is…" Invite 2–3 to share. These become the accountability anchors for Unit 3.

Transition to Unit 3: Remind participants — "What we built today is the strategic destination. Unit 3 maps that destination through KISS and defines the OKRs that will measure our progress toward it."
Suggested time: 8–10 minutes.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Interrogative Anchor · What is strategy? What is strategic intent? What is Success in Practice?
slo: Articulate strategic intent in terms of what the organisation pursues, why, how and when.
Distinguish the direction an organisation sets from the future position that defines its success.

parts.title: 1.1 — Strategy Master Definition
content: Strategy is frequently used but rarely precisely defined. In the S2R® framework it has a specific applied definition — every word carries strategic weight.

"Strategy is the output of iterative thinking, logic and process to determine what, why, how and when an organisation creates, delivers and sustains value to its stakeholders while navigating the forces within its operating environment."
✍✎ Reflection — The Definition
Which element of the master definition is least clearly present in your organisation's current strategy? What is the consequence of its absence?
prompts: ✍✎ Reflection — The Definition Which element of the master definition is least clearly present in your organisation's current strategy? What is the consequence of its absence?

parts.title: 1.2 — Strategic Intent: The 3W1H Framework
content: Critical Insight: Most strategies fail because HOW and WHEN are underdeveloped. HOW must include the full operating model and capability architecture. WHEN must address market timing, pivot triggers, and sequencing.
Dimension 1
WHAT
Dimension 2
WHY
Dimension 3
HOW
Dimension 4
WHEN
✍✎ Reflection — Strategic Intent
From your assigned executive leader perspective: which dimension (WHAT, WHY, HOW, WHEN) is least clearly defined in your organisation's current strategy? What would clarifying it change?
prompts: ✍✎ Reflection — Strategic Intent From your assigned executive leader perspective: which dimension (WHAT, WHY, HOW, WHEN) is least clearly defined in your organisation's current strategy? What would clarifying it change?

parts.title: 1.3 — Success in Practice (SiP): From Intent to Future Reality
content: The shift: from planning to experiencing. From "What are we going to do?" to "If this works, what will it look like in reality?" The team is positioned inside the future.
The 3W1H must show up in lived form across four observable domains:
How the value is experienced by customers
Why stakeholders trust, choose, and advocate for you
How the organisation actually operates (rhythm, coordination, capability)
The pace, sequencing, and responsiveness visible in execution
"If our strategic intent is sound and our strategy works — what will the organisation actually look like, feel like, and perform like in practice?"
Headline — Strategic Vision Anchor
One sentence capturing the strategic destination. Leaders repeat it in meetings, town halls, and board discussions. Signals the destination without describing the route.
Storyline — Strategic Narrative
A narrative of how the organisation operates when success has been achieved, across four observable future-reality dimensions. Leaders describe an operating reality they intend to build.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Strategic Intent Must Precede Success Definition
sections.sub: Ignition Point · Why must intent be clear before success can be described? Why must both be co-created?
slo: Explain why strategic intent and the meaning of success must be co-created by the leadership team.
Recognise how a shared direction filters decisions throughout execution.

parts.title: 2.1 — Why Intent and SiP Must Be Co-Created
content: The Strategic Intent Statement and SiP are co-created by the leadership team. This is a strategic requirement.
Leaders agree on the destination through genuine shared construction.
Trade-offs become visible early — the tensions between functions surface in the room, before execution.
Collective ownership is built — the only ownership that sustains during execution pressure.
✍✎ Reflection — Co-Creation
Has strategic intent in your organisation been genuinely co-created, or distributed from the top? What evidence do you have — and what has been the consequence?
prompts: ✍✎ Reflection — Co-Creation Has strategic intent in your organisation been genuinely co-created, or distributed from the top? What evidence do you have — and what has been the consequence?

parts.title: 2.2 — The Strategy Engine: Thinking · Process · Iteration
content: Layer 1
Thinking Logic
Layer 2
Process

Iterative Nature

Where Most Organisations Fail: Most focus heavily on Process, add some Iteration, and largely ignore Thinking Logic — the quality of the reasoning itself. The result: well-structured, regularly reviewed, genuinely wrong decisions.

parts.title: 2.3 — Role of Intent & SiP in the S2R® Architecture
content: Intent and SiP serve three functions in the Strategy2Results® architecture. Click each to expand.
Strategic Alignment▼
Strategic Intent (WHAT + WHY)
Ensures every executive is pursuing the same domain with the same differentiating logic.
Success in Practice (SiP)
Ensures every executive can visualise and describe the same future operating state.
Decision Filter▼
Strategic Intent (WHAT + WHY)
Does this initiative sit within our chosen arena and reinforce our WHY? If not — why are we doing it?
Success in Practice (SiP)
Does this move us closer to the organisation we described in our SiP? If not — what must change?
Execution Coherence▼
Strategic Intent (WHAT + WHY)
Provides the logic that connects every functional mandate to the enterprise direction — the WHY that all HOWs must serve.
Success in Practice (SiP)
Describes the organisation as a functioning system, helping leaders see how their individual functions contribute to the collective outcome.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Intent Fragments & How SiP Reveals It
sections.sub: Locate Hot Zones · Where does strategic intent fragment? How do SiP dimensions make fragmentation visible?
slo: Identify the observable signals that show whether the intended future position is being realised.
Recognise where the dominance of a single perspective causes strategic intent to drift.

parts.title: 3.1 — The Four SiP Dimensions: Observable Indicators
content: Each SiP dimension is a multidimensional observable reality. These are the specific signals that tell an executive team whether the strategy is working in that domain.
D1 · Customer Experience & Value
D2 · Operational Capability
D3 · People & Culture
D4 · Enterprise Value

parts.title: 3.2 — SiP Flammables: Where Imbalance Creates Drift
content: When one dimension dominates the SiP narrative, the strategy narrows into a functional ambition that no longer describes the enterprise.

parts.title: 5.1 — Using Assessment Results: Defining Corrective Actions
content: The executive team uses the Strategy Maturity Assessment results from Section 4 to identify the most critical corrective actions required. The assessment score across all 26 areas reveals where the organisation's strategic capability is strongest — and where it is most fragile.

The corrective actions identified here become the inputs into your SiP Application Table below. Before completing your SiP dimensions, review your assessment results and identify the specific gaps that must be addressed for the strategy to succeed.
Maturity Assessment — Reference Score
Your Assessment Score

Corrective Actions Across the Four SiP Dimensions

What must change to close the gap between your current customer experience and your SiP vision?

parts.title: 5.2 — Your SiP Application: Four Dimensions from Your Role
content: Using the corrective actions defined above, each CXO now describes all four SiP dimensions from the perspective of their assigned executive role. Write in the present tense of the future — as if the strategy has already succeeded and the corrective actions have been implemented.

parts.title: 5.3 — SiP Headline & Storyline: Your Contribution
content: Having completed your four-dimensional SiP table, now distil your perspective into the two forms described in Section 1: a Headline (one sentence — the portable vision anchor) and a Storyline (a narrative description of the future organisation as if it already exists).
These two outputs — from every CXO — will be integrated by the facilitator to produce one shared Strategic Intent Statement and one co-owned SiP that represents the collective executive view.
SiP Headline — From Your Role's Perspective
One sentence. The strategic destination as you see it from your function. Memorable, directional, and written in the present tense of the future.
SiP Storyline — From Your Role's Perspective

A narrative description of the future organisation, written in the present tense of the future, structured across the four observable dimensions. This is a description of the organisation as it already exists when the strategy has worked.

parts.title: 5.4 — Integration Summary: The Emerging Collective View
content: Following the completion of all CXO perspectives, the facilitator leads a structured synthesis to identify the four dimensions of the collective view. Record your observations from this synthesis below.
Points of Convergence
Where did all CXO descriptions align? What does the organisation consistently look like across all perspectives?
Points of Tension
Where did perspectives contradict or compete? Which functions described incompatible futures?
Missing Dimensions
Which of the four SiP dimensions was inadequately described by any CXO? What is the collective blind spot?
Dominant Bias
Which functional perspective was over-represented in the collective narrative? What does this tell the team about their strategic blind spots?
✍✎ Reflection — Application

Having completed the full application exercise — what is the single most important shift your organisation must make to close the gap between your current strategic capability and the SiP you have collectively described?

Missing Dimensions Which of the four SiP dimensions was inadequately described by any CXO? What is the collective blind spot? — Record the dimensions that no executive adequately described in the collective picture...

Dominant Bias Which functional perspective was over-represented in the collective narrative? What does this tell the team about their strategic blind spots? — Record which functional perspective dominated and what this means for the collective strategy...
